item.title: Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax
item.description:
Chengdu Rongcheng have won just two of their past 13 league matches. Photograph: Zhizhao Wu/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Chengdu Rongcheng have won just two of their past 13 league matches. Photograph: Zhizhao Wu/Getty Images
Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax
John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff
With four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.
The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points.AFC postpones Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia to late 2027 due to conflict in Middle East
Read more
They had been punished as part of a “special campaign to crack down on match-fixing, gambling and corruption in the football industry”, said a joint statement from the Chinese Football Association, the Ministry of Public Security and the General Administration of Sport at the time.
Chengdu were one of the seven to start on zero, above the defending champions Shanghai Port, who lost five points, and the runners-up Shanghai Shenhua who were hit with 10. It robbed the usual favourites of energy and it was all a bit surreal.
It almost felt over as soon as it started with Chengdu opening up a big lead, dropping just two points from the first 12 games while the usual powers struggled to get going.

item.title: China’s first AI-generated film is a flop. Some still see it as the future of cinema
item.description:
Sanxingdui: Future Past is China’s first AI-generated film released in Beijing but failed at the box office. Photograph: Wu Hao/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Sanxingdui: Future Past is China’s first AI-generated film released in Beijing but failed at the box office. Photograph: Wu Hao/EPAAnalysis
China’s first AI-generated film is a flop. Some still see it as the future of cinema Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
Chinese investors placing high value on AI despite unpopularity of Sanxingdui: Future Past
China’s first fully AI-generated movie has flopped, earning just 1.7m yuan (£191,000) at the box office despite costing “tens of millions” to make, according to its producer.
But is it any good? The Guardian watched Sanxingdui: Future Past in a virtually empty cinema in Beijing, and found it no worse than plenty of human-centred mindless action flicks.
OK, well maybe a bit worse.
Sanxingdui tells a confusing tale of a future society in which every decision has been outsourced to algorithms and AI, leading to a global catastrophe. The only way to avert the impending doom is to unlock the hidden code that is hidden in the Sanxingdui, bronze sculptures linked to the ancient kingdom of Shu. Cue astronauts racing through ancient Egypt and archeologists diving through space-time vortices.
Use of the production company’s in-house AI scriptwriting tool, called Bowen, was evident in lines such as, “That is the superbrain superintelligence that costs $10m dollars a month to subscribe to”, and, “Avoid that thing!” when a plane was about to crash in an incident foretold by the evil algorithm. But the sole other audience member and I agreed that it exceeded our very low expectations.
All of the film’s visuals and some of its sound effects were created using AI, while it was edited by humans.

item.title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
item.description:
Oman's sultan, Haitham bin Tariq, is led past an honour guard by China’s president, Xi Jinping, during a state visit to Beijing on Monday. Photograph: Sultan of Oman press office/APA Images/Shutterstock
View image in fullscreen
Oman's sultan, Haitham bin Tariq, is led past an honour guard by China’s president, Xi Jinping, during a state visit to Beijing on Monday. Photograph: Sultan of Oman press office/APA Images/ShutterstockAnalysis
Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with B...

item.title: Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boom
item.description:
Chang Yuequan with a photo of the gold haul from one of his mines the previous day worth £20,000 Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian
View image in fullscreen
Chang Yuequan with a photo of the gold haul from one of his mines the previous day worth £20,000 Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian
Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boom
Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports
The pork belly hits the oil with a sizzle, and a rich aroma of soy sauce and caramelising sugar fills the kitchen. Zhang Changchun, a middle-aged man from China’s Heilongjiang province, is cooking dinner for his friends on a warm evening in Mayaya, a small town in the Bolivian Amazon.
“Bolivia is my happy place,” he says in Mandarin as he adds the dish to a table overflowing with pork trotters, duck wings and braised sábalo fish. In this small restaurant, a group of half a dozen Chinese men gathers most nights to eat, drink and play mahjong.
View image in fullscreen
Zhang Changchun, a Chinese chef and mine investor, at dinner in Mayaya, Bolivia. Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian
Each man plays a critical role in the town’s booming gold business. Some work as investors or miners; others import supplies and equipment. Together, they run most of the town’s mining operations: about 20 open-pit mines and 12 dredge boats, operated by about 2,000 Bolivian and 200 Chinese workers.
The table gets rowdy as the men debate their afternoon games over high-end Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer. Almost every conversation revolves around money.
In less than a decade, private Chinese mining companies have turned this once-remote Amazonian town into a hub of gold speculation. Mining equipment stores, hotels and Chinese restaurants now line the main street.

item.title: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
item.description:
Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.
That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national securi...

item.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
item.description:
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesAnalysis
The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading Eduardo Porter
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.

item.title: It’s closer to Beijing than Washington – and residents of this Alaskan outpost are reeling from Trump’s policies
item.description:
Unalaska, in the Aleutian Islands, is further west than Hawaii, and most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage. Photograph: Brian Adams/The Guardian
View image in fullscreen
Unalaska, in the Aleutian Islands, is further west than Hawaii, and most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage. Photograph: Brian Adams/The Guardian
It’s closer to Beijing than Washington – and residents of this Alaskan outpost are reeling from Trump’s policies
On the Bering Sea, Unalaska is the US’s most productive seafood port, employing thousands of workers. But Trump’s cuts, and his disastrous war with Iran, have caused chaos – and put Republican control of Congress at risk
It was less than 17 hours until the start of Alaska’s lucrative Bering Sea crab season, and Oystein Lone was standing on a dock in the city of Unalaska, preparing to embark in rough conditions.
The problem wasn’t the next day’s forecast of 60mph gusts, which would kick up white-capped swells and make crabbing, already one of the most dangerous jobs in the United States, even more hazardous. Nor was it the question of whether there would be enough red king, tanner and snow crabs to go around – state regulators had, in fact, announced higher quotas for the season.
What was bothering Lone, as the sun sank lower in the sky that Wednesday evening, was the question of how to make the numbers work when diesel cost more than ever, thanks to the war with Iran.
“This is the most challenging time I’ve seen,” said Lone, who has been fishing since 1989. He had already spent $86,000 to put 12,000 gallons of the fuel in one of his two boats, but the price had climbed higher since then, and if he wanted to fill up again, he expected to spend $100,000.

item.title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
item.description:
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood. Photograph: Ng Han Guan/AP
View image in fullscreen
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood. Photograph: Ng Han Guan/AP
Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts
Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

item.title: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
item.description:
Members of the Politburo Standing Committee including Xi Jinping at the fifth plenum. Beijing has purged a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP). Photograph: Li Xiang/Xinhua/AP
View image in fullscreen
Members of the Politburo Standing Committee including Xi Jinping at the fifth plenum. Beijing has purged a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP). Photograph: Li Xiang/Xinhua/AP
China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
Read more
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.

item.title: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
item.description:
Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU technology conference on 21 October 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU technology conference on 21 October 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
Read more
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.

item.title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry
item.description:
Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’

The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.

item.title: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey
item.description:
Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining

It’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

item.title: Kylian Mbappé apologises after being dropped by Chinese brands for Mao Zedong comment
item.description:
• Video appears to show Mao Zedong called a ‘dictator’

  • Dongpeng and Mengniu end deals with the player

Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.

The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.

item.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
item.description:
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
